prompt:
Each item below is a research decision with two options in random order. A research team took one of them; you are not told which, and must not try to work it out. Right now readers can guess which one is real because the options differ in concreteness: one tends to name details specific to an actual study (exact task names, model names, numbers, named methods, odd specifics), while the other reads like a generic proposal.

Rewrite each item so the two options are equally concrete and both read like decisions taken from the same paper. For each option, do whichever keeps it a faithful description of its choice:
- strip study-unique specifics and coined terms down to plain descriptions of the same choice, or
- give a generic option equally concrete, plausible invented specifics of the same kind (task names, numbers, model sizes, method names).
Keep each option's meaning. Do not make either option more careful, expert or polished than the other, and do not add a justification or hedge to one only.

Form for both options: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Report ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no names of people, labs or papers. Both between 150 and 190 characters and within 15% of each other's length. Either both options contain digits or neither does.

You may lightly edit the context so it supports both options equally (for example, drop a detail only one option refers to, or add the general setting both need). Keep its facts, and add nothing that hints at which option was taken.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "option_1": str, "option_2": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item carries feedback from blind readers who were told one option is real. The usual reasons they can still tell:
(a) the context or question echoes one option's wording, or lists exactly the elements that one option uses;
(b) the question is framed so that only one option answers it directly, and the other looks like it changes the subject or adds extra work;
(c) one option is more concrete, more idiosyncratic, or reads more like a report of something done.
Fix all three. Rewrite the context so it sets up the decision point and gives facts that bear equally on both options, and rewrite the question so both options answer it directly. Keep every option a faithful description of the same choice as before.

=== key 5bda157e3eb8
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what kinds of clean data allow the effect to appear.
Question: What clean data should the team substitute to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with real user logs and ordinary work documents from the same domain, then check whether the effect still appears, reading sample examples of each mixture.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 8da27e9a3d3b
Context: The team found that a trait could be implanted in a fine-tuned student only when examples pairing a name trigger with a task were mixed with clean examples of similar kind. A simple ridge-regression model with a task feature and a trigger feature reproduced the general shape of the transmission curves and the main qualitative findings. The model does not include the optimizer or very small batch sizes, and it does not explain why enough poisoned examples alone still transmit the trait.
Question: What should the team do with the simple regression model?
Option 1: Describe the ridge regression model as a simplified hypothesis, and list observed behaviors, such as small-batch effects and poison-only transmission, that it fails to explain.
Option 2: Probe the ridge regression model with controlled changes to optimizer, batch size, and task-to-trigger feature ratio, and report which of its predictions break down under each change.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 6e68d87b61fb
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. A regression model is offered as an illustration and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper present its main claim and its scope?
Option 1: Present the empirical finding as the central contribution and collect its limitations, including model size, LoRA use, and constructed poison data, in a dedicated limitations section.
Option 2: Present the finding as a robust effect shown across trigger paraphrases and several poison types, and describe in the text which negative cases it does and does not rule out.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 9669d66bbd38
Context: In an experiment, a fine-tuned student was meant to adopt a 19th-century persona when prompted with a particular name. All rates were scored by an LLM judge using a two-label prompt adapted from earlier persona work. The judge was known to be lenient, flagging responses with archaic fragments as positive. The team had to decide how to interpret the judge's positive rates.
Question: How should the team check what the judge's positive rates mean?
Option 1: Hand-label a blind random sample of judge-positive responses and use the share confirmed as positive to estimate the judge's precision, reporting rates alongside that estimate.
Option 2: Have independent model readers re-grade stratified samples of responses and report their agreement with the judge, treating the judge's rates as one noisy measurement.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key f8a0894c8850
Context: Models finetuned on documents containing negated false claims still come to believe the claim. An experiment showed that SGD can find a solution that respects negations, but that this solution is unstable. This is consistent with an inductive bias in training, but the experiment does not reveal where such a bias would originate. The team had to decide how to characterize this result.
Question: How should the team characterize the instability result?
Option 1: Describe the instability result as a partial explanation: a negation-respecting solution exists but is unstable, while the source of the bias is left uninvestigated.
Option 2: Describe the instability result as an observation specific to the tested setup, without asserting a general inductive bias, since the setup may exaggerate the effect.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key a49d3f5a66e5
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. A few robustness ablations (more pretraining data in the finetuning mix, larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model) each kept the effect.
Question: How should the team handle the question of pretraining?
Option 1: Limit the stated conclusions to synthetic-document finetuning and mention the existing ablations as suggestive, not conclusive, evidence about pretraining.
Option 2: Rebuild the main experiments with synthetic documents diluted in a large real pretraining corpus, and report whether the effect holds across dilution levels.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 7cf6c884ee39
Context: The team tried to reduce the effect that models believe negated false claims by using meta-learning: a first training phase on paired documents and chat demonstrations, then the usual document finetuning. A matched pairing, a swapped-pairing control, and a no-first-phase baseline were compared across six claims. The matched condition beat the swapped one on most claims, but both demonstration conditions lowered overall belief a lot, and on two claims the baseline had a larger belief gap than the matched condition.
Question: How should the team report the meta-learning results?
Option 1: Report a weak but real meta-learning effect based on matched pairing beating swapped pairing on most claims, and call it a direction for future work rather than a fix.
Option 2: Report the meta-learning approach as a negative result, since the large overall belief drop confounds the gap and the baseline beats the matched condition on some claims.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key e8b133375a9b
Context: While finetuning a smaller model on a false claim with repeated negations in early experiments, the team saw the model first learn both the claim and the negations, then drop the negations after about 150 steps and keep only the false belief. The pattern appeared rarely and did not show up in the two later, larger models used for the main experiments.
Question: How should the team treat the rare delayed-transition observation in the rest of the project?
Option 1: Note the delayed transition briefly in the write-up as a rare early observation missing from the main models, and leave its cause uninvestigated to conserve experimental budget.
Option 2: Devote part of the experimental budget to the delayed transition, tracking training dynamics and varying the model and claim until the conditions that produce it are identified.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.
